title: Story-Scene Loose Parts
strapline: Pebbles for stepping stones, blue cloth for the river, corks for the villagers — build the world of a story and play it out.
intent: Children retell and invent stories, building the setting from open-ended parts and moving the characters through it.
Children think symbolically — a fir cone is a troll, a scarf is a river, the child assigns the meaning.
Children sequence a narrative with a beginning, middle and end, and talk it aloud as they play.
Children use rich story language and new vocabulary from the tales they know.
Children collaborate on a shared world, negotiating who is who and what happens next.
implementation: Provide a base — a tray, a cloth, a wooden frame — and open-ended parts: pebbles, cones, corks, scarves, sticks, gems.
Read or retell a well-loved story first, then invite children to build its world with the loose parts.
Follow the child's meaning — if a button is the gingerbread man, it is, and it runs.
Model story language and narration, then hand the telling back: 'and then what happened?'
Add small figures, animals and story stones to spark small-world retelling and invention.
Photograph the scenes children build and turn them into a class-made storybook.
Let children invent entirely new stories in the built world, not just retell the given one.
key_questions: What could this be in your story?
What happens at the beginning — and how does it end?
Who lives in the world you've built?
What does your character do next?
Shall we photograph your scene and turn it into a book?

impact.text: Children retell familiar stories with props and invent their own variations.
Children think symbolically, assigning meaning to open-ended parts in the scene.
Children sequence a narrative with a beginning, middle and end and narrate it aloud.
Children use rich story language and new vocabulary from the tales they know.
Children collaborate on a shared story-world, negotiating roles and what happens next.
Children place small parts and figures precisely as they compose the scene.

enhancements: A tray, cloth or wooden frame as the story base.
Open-ended parts — pebbles, cones, corks, scarves, sticks, gems.
Small figures, animals and story stones to move through the scene.
Blue cloth for water, brown for paths, green for forests.
Story stones painted with characters and settings.
A camera and a blank book for turning scenes into class stories.
A basket of well-loved books beside the collection for inspiration.

playing_exploring: Children pour the stories they love into worlds they build themselves.
The same loose parts become a beanstalk, a bridge and a beach in one week.
active_learning: Children stay with a story-world, developing and replaying it over time.
They keep building until the scene is right for the tale.
creating_thinking: Assigning meaning to objects is early abstract, symbolic thinking.
Children invent new plots and solve what happens next together.
